extracted.intended_audience: parliamentarians, government policymakers, regulatory agencies, and administrative law practitioners (Canadian context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for how administrative agencies should make regulations and how executive 'policy directions' should be used, including when to give agencies autonomy, how to conduct consultation/notice-and-comment, and what parliamentary oversight is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable opportunity to participate (notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'reasonable', the opportunity to participate should be genuine, commensurate with the importance of the issue, open, equally available to competing interests, and sufficiently early in the process to be meaningful, without crippling the agency in the fulfilment of its overall objectives by introducing unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ways must be found to offset the cost of participation where necessary (e.g., direct government funding; cost awards; economic support to legal service groups; government representation by public advocacy officers). The notice-and-comment process must not be merely ceremonial but have practical significance (example: Canada Post deciding definition of 'letter' in practice before statutory notice-and-comment undermined participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate legislation as a useful regulatory mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate legislative process can be more dynamic, responsive, open to direct participation and more efficient than the parliamentary process; it allows expression of durable objectives while leaving flexibility to administrative regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can help Parliament concentrate on essentials, avoid reopening whole policy debates over particular clauses, and avoid needless repetition of policy arguments. But it is not universally applicable (some specialized adjudicative functions find the concept foreign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Instruments Act preliminary screening criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Statutory Instruments Act, regulations filed in advance are scrutinized for vires, unusual use of authority, undue encroachment on the rights of individuals, and quality of drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations are registered and published; all statutory instruments are referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments for further scrutiny respecting drafting quality, vires, human rights, and, to some extent, merits. The screening process focuses on form but can have substantive implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt agency-made regulations that undergo notice-and-comment from preliminary central screening (pilot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency regulations submitted to a public notice-and-comment procedure could be exempted from the Statutory Instruments Act requirements that precede registration and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: those most directly affected will act as scrutineers; exemption could reduce duplication and bottlenecks at central offices and free central drafters to concentrate on government regulations. Tradeoffs: may reduce uniformity of language/format; categories in the Act might need broadening; pilot project suggested to test the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to vest regulation-making autonomy in agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the enabling statute mixes policy determination with decision making, there are reasons for leaving policy determination to the agency rather than the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three reasons: (1) routine executive involvement may compromise decision integrity; (2) authoritativeness accorded to the agency enhances the quality of public participation; (3) technical or peripheral matters are inefficient for Cabinet to handle. But overriding considerations (sensitivity, human rights, major economic impact) may warrant executive control; no hard-and-fast rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary oversight and a generalized disallowance procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should oversee regulations and agencies should account to Parliament; a general procedure allowing Parliament to disallow subordinate legislation (without amendment) would reinforce accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbolic benefit: reinforces Parliament as supreme arbiter subject to Constitution. Functional benefit: Parliament provides forum for discussion and can promote compliance through politics of reason/embarrassment. Implementation details (how to avoid excessive parliamentary time or manipulation) are left to parliamentary rules or committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of 'directions' / policy statements (four concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish four concepts: (1) informal policy statements (non‑statutory expressions of purpose); (2) administrative 'directives' (internally binding but not justiciable); (3) binding policy statements that self-limit discretion and are enforceable by courts; (4) directions that are regulatory in nature and bind all where statute provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity in classification is essential because legal status (justiciable/enforceable) and expectations of parties depend on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow parameters for issuing policy directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy directions should be used only within narrow parameters: to address general policy issues in advance of specific cases and not to change rules mid‑proceeding or to affect individual adjudicative decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They should be viewed as legislation, not 'decisions'; Parliament should authorize executive control only over agencies with broad mandates and where statute-by-statute determination deems it suitable; directions should not be issued to agencies performing solely adjudicative or courtlike functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form directions as regulations and apply statutory safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy directions should take the form of regulations so their legislative character is clear and statutory safeguards apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: directions would be subject to the Statutory Instruments Act (publication in Canada Gazette; tabled in Parliament; scrutiny by Standing Joint Committee), create a presumption against retrospective application, and reduce the risk of creating unenforceable expectations. Agencies could initiate the process; consider retaining a revocation power for the executive. 'Freeze' orders (ninety-day) are favoured to suspend new applications while policy is developed; 'stop' orders halting ongoing proceedings are disfavoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on changing rules during ongoing applications (avoid interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions intended to influence policy questions that arise in the context of an existing application risk changing the rules in the midst of the proceeding and are viewed with abhorrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop orders to halt proceedings are viewed as blatant interference; freeze orders (temporary suspension of new applications or short freezes) are less intrusive and may be justified in limited form (90 days previously recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation requirement before issuing directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions should be issued only after an appropriate measure of consultation, particularly where they effect a substantial policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum for consultation should be flexible (agency, department, parliamentary committee, royal commission, or other inquiry) and chosen by context. There should always be a public record of views of participants against which the executive policy can be measured. Current practice 'rarely gives interested persons an opportunity to influence government policy'—this should be remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints on agency rights to request directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although agencies would be able to initiate the process for political direction, agencies should not be given a formal right to require the Government to issue a direction or create a duty for the Government to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting a right to request a direction could imply a duty on the Government to respond; the Report disagrees with proposals to allow agencies or parties to compel the Government to issue directions (example: opposition to Bill C-20 amendment relating to CRTC). Agencies may still approach Cabinet through normal political channels.
